documents.title: AAPOS vision screening recommendations for children

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This study shows that children from both below-average and above-average median household income (MHI) areas experience high rates of vision screening failure, uncorrected refractive errors and spectacle needs. While the demand for vision care services is evident in both groups, children from below-average MHI areas exhibit higher rates and a greater overall need. These findings highlight the necessity for mobile school-based vision screening initiatives, such as our University of California, Irvine EyeMobile programme, to provide free, equitable and readily accessible vision care for school children. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY These findings highlight the urgent need to expand school-based vision screening programmes to serve children from all socio-economic backgrounds, with a particularly significant impact in low-income areas. By implementing and supporting such programmes, policymakers and healthcare providers can make a substantial positive difference in their communities. Early interventions can improve paediatric eye health and academic performance, potentially reducing disability rates, boosting productivity and enhancing the overall quality of life for all community members. Introduction School-based and mobile vision programmes are increasingly used to reduce barriers to paediatric eye care access, particularly in underserved communities; however, socio-economic factors continue to influence visual outcomes through differences in access to care, awareness and timely treatment. It remains unclear whether disparities in visual acuity (VA), refractive error prevalence and spectacle provision persist when cost and accessibility barriers are minimised through community-based services. Understanding these patterns is important for evaluating the effectiveness of equity-focused healthcare delivery models and informing public health strategies aimed at reducing preventable childhood visual impairment. Children from low-income backgrounds in particular show higher rates of undiagnosed vision disorders and uncorrected refractive errors, which can lead to long-term academic disadvantages and developmental delay. The University of California, Irvine (UCI) EyeMobile, in providing free screenings, examinations and glasses, has generated a comprehensive dataset for examining how community socio-economic factors can affect rates of paediatric visual impairment. This retrospective cross-sectional study of comprehensive eye examination data from 2021 to 2024 investigates the rates of visual impairment that are uncovered when barriers to care in accessibility and costs are mitigated through a free mobile school-based vision screening programme. VA, refractive error prevalence and spectacle prescription rates were compared between children living in communities above and below the average household income of Orange County, California, USA. Materials and methods Patients and data collection The UCI Institutional Review Board (IRB) Committee granted an exemption from IRB review, as the study did not meet the criteria for human subject research (IRB #1152). All data were fully de-identified prior to investigator access, and no protected health information was included in the analytical dataset. The study was conducted in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) regulations and the ethical standards set by the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki. Children aged 3–10 were eligible for inclusion, while exclusion criteria applied to those who were absent during screening, lacked parental consent for a comprehensive follow-up evaluation or were already under optometric care. For three consecutive academic years from 2021 to 2024, including summer school, 15 842 children received vision screenings at locations throughout Orange County, including preschools, Head Start and elementary schools. Screening was conducted across 285 public school sites over the three academic years. Of these, 68 schools were located in areas with above-average median household income (MHI), and 217 in areas with below-average MHI, based on the school’s zip code. All participating schools were public institutions; no private schools were included. Because public school attendance in California is largely determined by residential zoning, school location closely reflects neighbourhood socio-economic conditions. Therefore, the school-level MHI was used as a proxy for community socio-economic status (SES) in this study. Refractive error determination Emmetropia, hyperopia and myopia were based on spherical equivalent (SE), calculated as spherical error (SPH) plus half cylindrical error (CYL). All refractive error measurements were determined by Retinomax K-Plus 3 Autorefractor (Righton, Tokyo, Japan). Data from retinoscopy under cycloplegia were used if available. Hyperopia was defined as SE ≥ +0.50 dioptre (D), myopia as SE ≤ –0.50 D and emmetropia as –0.50 D<SE < +0.50 D. Astigmatism was defined as CYL ≤ –0.50 D. Anisometropia was defined as an interocular difference in SE ≥1.00 D. The severity of refractive error, based on absolute SE for myopia or hyperopia and based on absolute CYL for astigmatism, was categorised as: mild (0.50–1.75 D), moderate (2.00–3.75 D), moderately severe (4.00–5.75 D), severe (≥6.00 D). Screening Initial screening was performed using the Retinomax K-Plus 3 Autorefractor (Righton). Children were referred for free comprehensive eye examination in the UCI EyeMobile clinic on meeting the following screening criteria: SPH ≥ +1.75 D or SPH ≤ –3.25 D, CYL ≤ –1.50 D or interocular difference with ΔSPH

CYL ≤ –0.50 D. Anisometropia was defined as an interocular difference in SE ≥1.00 D. The severity of refractive error, based on absolute SE for myopia or hyperopia and based on absolute CYL for astigmatism, was categorised as: mild (0.50–1.75 D), moderate (2.00–3.75 D), moderately severe (4.00–5.75 D), severe (≥6.00 D). Screening Initial screening was performed using the Retinomax K-Plus 3 Autorefractor (Righton). Children were referred for free comprehensive eye examination in the UCI EyeMobile clinic on meeting the following screening criteria: SPH ≥ +1.75 D or SPH ≤ –3.25 D, CYL ≤ –1.50 D or interocular difference with ΔSPH ≥1.50 D or with ΔCYL ≥1.00 D. Children who passed the autorefractor vision screening but required new spectacles with their current prescription were fitted for new frames. These referral thresholds were based on established paediatric vision screening protocols used in school-based programmes during the study period and were designed to identify refractive errors associated with amblyopia risk factors requiring further ophthalmic evaluation. Instrument-based screening approaches using autorefractors and photoscreeners are widely recommended for paediatric vision screening programmes and have been standardised through guidelines from the American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus (AAPOS). Updated screening recommendations from the AAPOS were published during the study period; however, the criteria used in this programme remained consistent with established referral practices for identifying children requiring further evaluation. Comprehensive eye examination On receipt of parental informed consent, children received a comprehensive eye examination from one of three paediatric optometrists at the UCI EyeMobile clinic. Uncorrected and best-corrected VA (UCVA and BCVA) testing was performed using one of the following VA charts, based on the child’s age, cooperation or intellectual capability: the Lea symbol chart, HOTV matching chart or Snellen chart. VA was calculated as the logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution (logMAR), or the negative log of the VA score. Next, refraction testing was performed using the Retinomax autorefractor, phoropter and retinoscopy, both with and without cycloplegia, as administered at the discretion of the examining optometrist. All children had received a non-cycloplegic refraction measurement by Retinomax autorefractor and retinoscopy. Cycloplegia was attained using a drop of phenylephrine (2.5%) and tropicamide (1%). Cycloplegic refraction assessment was performed 30 min after induction of dilation. The examination also included: pupillary light reflex test, ocular motility examination, Titmus stereoacuity test, colour vision test using the Good-Lite ColorCheck Complete Vision Screener and cover test with distance (20 feet) and near (40 cm) fixation. The anterior segment was examined by slit lamp, while the fundus examination was done by binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy. If detected on the cover test, strabismus was further evaluated by prism and alternate cover test. If BCVA was 20/40 or worse, an updated spectacle prescription and a new pair of spectacles were provided at no cost. Parents and children were instructed on proper and effective spectacle use. Children requiring further evaluation with the Baylor-Video Acuity Tester or referral to ophthalmology were identified based on clinical findings during the examination and were referred accordingly. Criteria for referral to ophthalmology included but were not limited to detection of the following: strabismus, cataracts, keratoconus, corneal abrasion, abnormal red reflex, nystagmus, uveitis and/or retinal or optical dystrophies. Data analysis A retrospective cross-sectional study analysed comprehensive eye examination records over three consecutive academic years, including an interim summer session, from 2021 to 2024. A total of 3350 children were evaluated following initial vision screening failures. Local MHI data were sourced from the US Census Bureau and the Internal Revenue Service database, categorised by school zip code. The relative MHI (rMHI) was computed as the ratio of the local MHI to the overall MHI for Orange County. Local MHI values were determined using each school site’s zip code, serving as a proxy for SES. Participants were categorised into two groups: those with above-average income (rMHI ≥1.0) and those with below-average income (rMHI <1.0). While zip code-level MHI is a commonly used surrogate in public health research, it may not accurately capture individual-level socio-economic variation and can introduce ecological fallacy. This limitation is acknowledged, and future studies may benefit from integrating more granular household-level SES data where available. The distribution of examined children by rMHI is shown in . Following rMHI categorisation, UCVA and BCVA data in logMAR units were stratified from sharp to low VA: <0.2 (20/30 or better), 0.3–0.4 (20/40–20/50), 0.5–0.6 (20/60–20/80) and >0.7 (20/100 or worse). For each rMHI category, the rates of emmetropia, myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism and anisometropia were determined according to earlier definitions. Myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism were further stratified by severity into categories specified earlier. For each rMHI category, the spectacle provision rates were also determined, reporting those who required a new or updated prescription, along with new frames or only required new frames. Results were reported as the mean with SE. Statistical analyses were performed using

Myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism were further stratified by severity into categories specified earlier. For each rMHI category, the spectacle provision rates were also determined, reporting those who required a new or updated prescription, along with new frames or only required new frames. Results were reported as the mean with SE. Statistical analyses were performed using Python (V.3.10). Pandas was used for data cleaning and manipulation; NumPy for array operations and descriptive statistics; SciPy for inferential statistics, including t-tests and χ² tests; and the statistics module for additional summary statistics and variance calculations. ORs with 95% CIs were calculated for selected comparative outcomes to quantify associations between income group and vision-related outcomes. Statistical significance was defined as p<0.05. Results From 2021 to 2024, a total of 15 842 students were evaluated in the UCI EyeMobile programme. They were divided into two groups based on their MHI: those with a below-average score (n=11 112) and those with an above-average score (n=4730). Of those, 22.8% (n=3609) did not meet screening criteria and were referred for comprehensive ophthalmological examinations, including 24.6% (n=2735) from below-average and 18.5% (n=874) from above-average MHI groups. Children from below-average MHI areas had significantly higher odds of screening failure compared with those from above-average MHI areas (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.33 to 1.57). Additionally, 5.2% (n=825) required new eyewear, with 5.2% (n=576) from those with below-average MHI and 5.3% (n=249) from those with above-average MHI. Only 0.4% (n=59) passed while using previous EyeMobile spectacles. Finally, 0.9% (n=150) could not be screened for various reasons, including 1.0% (n=110) from the below-average MHI group and 0.8% (n=40) from the above-average MHI group. Demographics data The demographic breakdown of screened students showed that most identified as Hispanic (51.7%), followed by Caucasian (23.5%) and Asian (16.7%) ( ). In the below-average MHI group, 56.4% (n=6271) were Hispanic, compared with 40.6% (n=1922) in the above-average MHI group. Caucasian students were more prevalent in the above-average MHI group (33.2%, n=1568) than in the below-average group (19.3%, n=2150). Asian student proportions were consistent across groups, with 16.7% (n=1855) below average and 16.8% (n=795) above average. Regarding preferred language, 23.7% (n=3760) preferred Spanish; in the below-average group, 24% (n=2664) preferred Spanish, compared with 23.2% (n=1096) in the above-average group, showing a minimal difference ( ). A total of 11 199 students were seen at the EyeMobile clinic for comprehensive eye examinations following their initial vision screenings. Among these, 3350 students underwent complete cycloplegic refraction examinations, allowing for more accurate assessment of refractive errors. These students were categorised based on the rMHI of their school’s zip code into below-average and above-average MHI groups. Of the 3350 students with complete data, 45.4% were found to have normal vision. When stratified by income group, 46.0% of children in the below-average MHI group and 42.6% in the above-average MHI group demonstrated normal VA. In contrast, 19.3% of all eye examinations were conducted without cycloplegic dilation, typically due to logistical or parental consent limitations. This subset included 18.8% of students from below-average MHI areas and 21.8% from above-average MHI areas ( ). The primary refractive error analyses were conducted using the subset of children who underwent complete cycloplegic refraction, minimising the potential impact of non-cycloplegic measurements on the main study outcomes. The proportion of non-dilated examinations was similar across income groups, reducing the likelihood of systematic bias between socio-economic categories. Additionally, 16.4% of students were determined to require and be eligible for spectacle correction based on refractive error and clinical judgement. The proportion of students prescribed glasses was comparable between the two income groups, as shown in . Visual acuity data This analysis included a total of 3350 subjects: 2722 (81.3%) from below-average MHI areas and 628 (18.7%) from above-average MHI areas. The mean age was 5.97±2.18 years, with a median age of 5 years for both groups. The spectacle prescription rate was 69.3%, higher in the below-average MHI group at 70.3% (1913/2722) compared with 64.8% (407/628) in the above-average MHI group (table 5). Both distance and near UCVA displayed an exponential distribution of VA severity, with more children showing high VA (logMAR <0.2) and fewer with low VA (logMAR >0.7). After correction, the distribution steepened significantly, with more children showing improved VA, as anticipated. In terms of uncorrected distance VA (UDVA), 55.3% of examined eyes had acuity better than 20/30 (<0.2 logMAR). Specifically, 54.5% of individuals with a below-average MHI reached this level, while 59.1% in the above-average MHI group did. Among the groups, 24.8% of eyes with below-average MHI had acuity between 20/40–20/50 (0.3–0.4 logMAR), compared

After correction, the distribution steepened significantly, with more children showing improved VA, as anticipated. In terms of uncorrected distance VA (UDVA), 55.3% of examined eyes had acuity better than 20/30 (<0.2 logMAR). Specifically, 54.5% of individuals with a below-average MHI reached this level, while 59.1% in the above-average MHI group did. Among the groups, 24.8% of eyes with below-average MHI had acuity between 20/40–20/50 (0.3–0.4 logMAR), compared with 23.5% in the above-average group. Additionally, 11.9% of eyes in the below-average MHI group had acuity between 20/63–20/80 (0.5–0.6 logMAR), compared with 10.0% in the above-average MHI group. Finally, 8.8% of below-average MHI eyes had acuity worse than 20/100 (>0.7 logMAR), compared with 7.5% in the above-average group. Best-corrected distance VA (BCDVA) showed significant improvement in both groups compared with UDVA. An overall achievement rate of 84% was observed among participants who reached VA better than 20/30 (ie, <0.2 logMAR). Among spectacle users, 83.7% in the below-average group and 86.0% in the above-average group met this threshold. For BCDVA between 20/40–20/50 (0.3–0.4 logMAR), the rates were similar: 12.7% for below-average MHI versus 9.6% for above-average MHI. A small percentage achieved acuity levels of 20/63–20/80 (0.5–0.6 logMAR), with rates of about 2.4% for below-average and 2.5% for above-average MHI. Lastly, for BCDVA exceeding 0.7 logMAR, the rates were approximately 1.2% for below average MHI and 1.9% for above average MHI ( ). Refractive errors This analysis examined 5384 individual eyes (right and left eyes analysed separately), with 4384 (81.4%) from below-average MHI areas and 1000 (18.6%) from above-average MHI areas ( ). Percentages for refractive error categories were calculated based on the total number of eyes within each group unless otherwise specified. Emmetropia was seen in 36.9% of eyes; 37.2% in below-average MHI and 35.4% in above-average MHI. Myopia prevalence was 25.8%, with 74.7% of myopic eyes mild (0.50–1.99 D) and 88.7% with astigmatism. Hyperopia was found in 37.3% of eyes, higher in the above-average MHI group (38.8%) than in the below-average group (37%). Mild hyperopia accounted for 71% of cases, and concurrent astigmatism was more common in the below-average MHI group (80.9%) than in the above-average (64.7%). Overall, astigmatism affected 73.6% of eyes, with a higher rate in the below-average MHI group (75.3%) than in the above-average group (66.1%). The odds of astigmatism were significantly higher among children from below-average MHI areas compared with those from above-average areas (OR 1.56, 95% CI 1.36 to 1.79). Mild astigmatism was present in 59.5% of astigmatic eyes. Anisometropia (≥1.00 D difference) occurred in 9.1% of participants, with similar rates across income groups ( ). Among these, 79.3% had spherical anisometropia, 35.5% had cylindrical anisometropia and 85.5% had astigmatism. Spectacle rate The study results revealed significant rates of vision correction needs among the examined students. Out of 3350 students who underwent complete cycloplegic refraction examinations, 69.3% (2320 students) required new or updated prescriptions. This rate was higher in the below-average MHI group at 70.3% (1913 out of 2722 students) versus 64.8% (407 out of 628 students) in the above-average MHI group ( ). Children from below-average MHI areas also had higher odds of requiring spectacle prescription compared with those from above-average MHI areas (OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.56). 19% (637 students) of the total examined population required new eyeglass frames without a change in prescription (fit-for-frames). Distribution was similar across income groups, with 19.1% (520 students) in the below-average MHI group and 18.6% (117 students) in the above-average MHI group ( ). In total, 88.3% (2957 students) required spectacle intervention, with a higher proportion in the below-average MHI group at 89.4% (2433 students) than in the above-average group at 83.4% (524 students) ( ). Discussion The UCI EyeMobile for Children study, conducted across Orange County, California, USA, examined paediatric visual health within a region marked by substantial socio-economic heterogeneity. Although the county’s MHI is approximately US$100 485, this aggregate masks wide income variation: cities like Irvine and Newport Beach exceed US$120 000, while others, such as Santa Ana and Anaheim, fall below US$50 000 in specific zip codes. This geographical and economic diversity enabled the EyeMobile programme to reach a broad cross-section of communities, providing a unique opportunity to investigate how localised income disparities are associated with paediatric vision outcomes. By stratifying student data based on school zip code-level rMHI, the study assessed income-linked differences in screening failure rates, refractive error prevalence and spectacle provision. While zip code-level MHI is a proxy and does not capture individual-level variation, it remains a validated and widely used metric in public health research, especially in the absence of granular income data. By stratifying student data based on school zip code-level rMHI, the study assessed income-linked differences in screening failure rates, refractive error prevalence and spectacle provision. While zip code-level MHI is a proxy and does not capture individual-level variation, it remains a validated and widely used metric in public health research, especially in the absence of granular income data. In this context, its application was both practical and justified, aligning with the EyeMobile programme’s geographically distributed care model and the broader objective of advancing health equity. Importantly, this study was conducted within a mobile, school-based care model designed to reduce traditional barriers to paediatric eye care, including financial cost, transportation limitations and access to specialists. Within this study cohort, children from below-average MHI communities had greater unmet vision needs, poorer UCVA and higher rates of refractive errors requiring correction than children from above-average MHI communities. Because this study used a cross-sectional design, we were unable to evaluate whether unmet vision needs decreased following implementation of the EyeMobile programme or whether disparities in visual outcomes changed over time. These findings suggest that socio-economic disparities in paediatric visual health may persist even when access barriers are minimised, reflecting broader structural and environmental determinants influencing health outcomes. These trends are consistent with broader national data indicating that socio-economic disadvantage is closely linked to higher rates of uncorrected refractive errors and limited access to timely vision care. Limited access to paediatric eye examinations, financial constraints and systemic barriers such as transportation and insurance gaps may all contribute to delayed diagnosis and intervention. Importantly, our cross-sectional design limits any inference of causality; observed associations cannot establish temporal or causal relationships between SES and vision outcomes. Interestingly, children from above-average MHI areas also exhibited substantial vision care needs, including a higher prevalence of myopia. This may reflect increased near work and screen time, consistent with previous studies indicating a link between educational intensity and myopia prevalence. These findings emphasise the need for vision health interventions across the socio-economic spectrum, with targeted resource allocation in lower-income communities where the greatest need and access gaps exist. A key example of this disparity is spectacle provision: 70.3% of children in areas with a below-average MHI required new or updated prescriptions, compared with 64.8% in areas with an above-average MHI ( ). Additionally, 19.1% of lower-income children required new frames, compared with 18.6% in higher-income areas. These differences, while modest, reinforce the greater cumulative need in underserved populations. Prior research supports this pattern, showing that children in lower-income households often receive less routine vision care and are more likely to require first-time or corrective interventions. The UCI EyeMobile programme significantly improves access to spectacles for children in need; however, challenges such as frame fit and compliance remain, warranting further investigation. Children from lower-income communities may experience delays in receiving refractive correction and may also face challenges such as spectacle loss or breakage, which can reduce the overall effectiveness of these interventions. Moreover, economic and logistical barriers contribute to non-adherence to spectacle use, as prior studies have shown that cost and parental education about refractive errors influence children’s adherence to prescribed glasses. The demographic trends observed in our study reflect underlying disparities in access to paediatric eye care. Children from below-average MHI areas were more likely to identify as Hispanic. This group has historically experienced lower rates of routine eye examinations and higher rates of undiagnosed refractive errors, patterns linked to longstanding inequities in healthcare access. Interestingly, Spanish language preference was similar across income groups, suggesting that socio-economic barriers, not language alone, may be more influential in shaping disparities. Cultural beliefs, limited parental awareness about the importance of vision correction and logistical challenges such as transportation and work constraints may all contribute to reduced engagement with preventive eye care services, even when programmes are made available. These findings emphasise the need for public health interventions that are not only accessible but also culturally responsive and community-informed. Astigmatism represents a significant and often under-addressed contributor to visual impairment in children, particularly in low-income communities. Its prevalence may reflect not only genetic predisposition but also structural barriers to early detection and intervention. When uncorrected, astigmatism, especially when accompanied by hyperopia, can impair contrast sensitivity, delay visual development and negatively affect reading fluency and academic performance. Despite its impact, mild astigmatism frequently goes undetected in traditional school screenings, which often rely solely on VA charts and may miss subtle yet functionally significant refractive errors. When uncorrected, astigmatism, especially when accompanied by hyperopia, can impair contrast sensitivity, delay visual development and negatively affect reading fluency and academic performance. Despite its impact, mild astigmatism frequently goes undetected in traditional school screenings, which often rely solely on VA charts and may miss subtle yet functionally significant refractive errors. These challenges are particularly pronounced in lower-income populations, where access to routine paediatric eye examinations is often limited. Incorporating autorefractors such as the Retinomax K-Plus 3 into school-based screening programmes may help address these gaps by enabling objective, efficient and scalable detection of refractive errors. These findings support a growing call for policy shifts toward more comprehensive, refractive error-centred screening strategies in public schools, particularly in districts serving socio-economically disadvantaged children. From a public health perspective, the UCI EyeMobile is a mobile, school-based care model designed to reduce traditional barriers to paediatric eye care, including financial barriers, transportation challenges and limited access to specialists. Importantly, despite these reduced barriers, children from lower-income communities in our study continued to demonstrate greater unmet vision needs and higher rates of refractive error requiring correction. These findings suggest that socio-economic disparities in paediatric visual health may persist even when access barriers are minimised, highlighting the influence of broader structural and social determinants of health. Expanding school-based mobile vision programmes may therefore improve access while also requiring complementary strategies to address the underlying socio-economic factors that contribute to persistent disparities. Strengths of this study include a large and diverse sample, objective screening using the Retinomax autorefractor and direct spectacle provision to children who need them. However, several limitations warrant consideration. First, using zip code-level MHI as a proxy for individual SES may obscure within-area variability and introduce the risk of ecological fallacy. Although school-level MHI by zip code was used as a proxy for SES, this measure reflects community-level rather than individual-level income and may introduce ecological fallacy. However, because all participating schools were public institutions serving residentially defined catchment areas, school location likely provides a reasonable approximation of neighbourhood socio-economic conditions within this cohort. Without individual-level SES data, the strength of associations may be underestimated or confounded by unmeasured variables. Additionally, approximately 19% of examinations were performed without cycloplegia, which may introduce measurement variability, particularly by underestimating hyperopia due to accommodative effects. However, the primary refractive error analyses were conducted using the subset of children who underwent complete cycloplegic refraction, and the proportion of non-dilated examinations was similar across income groups, reducing the likelihood of differential bias. Second, the lack of long-term follow-up data limits the ability to assess sustained spectacle adherence and the lasting impact of vision correction. While immediate need was addressed, the long-term effectiveness of the intervention remains unclear without data on wear consistency, replacement access or academic outcomes. Third, a 7.2% no-show rate among children referred for further evaluation may introduce selection bias. These children may differ systematically from those who completed follow-up, potentially leading to an underestimation of unmet vision needs. This is particularly relevant in underserved populations, where barriers to follow-up care, such as transportation, parental availability or cost, are more pronounced. These factors collectively limit the generalisability of the findings and underscore the need for longitudinal data in future evaluations. Future research must explore strategies that enhance follow-up adherence and ensure the sustained benefits of vision correction. Incorporating qualitative assessments can reveal the barriers affecting consistent spectacle use among disadvantaged populations. Overall, this study reveals that paediatric uncorrected refractive error rates are high across all socio-economic backgrounds, and that children from lower-income areas experience even higher rates and a greater need for spectacles. These findings underscore the important role of UCI EyeMobile in expanding access to vision care, with profound benefits for all children, particularly those from underserved communities. Future research should investigate the long-term effects of early interventions on education, strategies to improve spectacle adherence and scalable models for integrating vision care into school health programmes.
